n: Job answers Bildad, but much of this speech is really about how to stand before God.
Yes, I know God is just. But how can any human be declared right before God? Job uses the language of a courtroom, a theme that runs through the book.

f.w: how should man be just with God?
f.g: How can a person win a legal case against God, or be declared innocent?

n: If someone tried to argue with God, he couldn’t answer even one question in a thousand.
God is all-wise and all-powerful. Who has ever defied Him and come out unharmed?
Job praises God’s power in a hymn-like passage (verses 5–10). God moves mountains before they know it and overturns them in His anger.
He shakes the earth from its place, and its foundations tremble — a picture of earthquakes.

f.g: Ancient poetic image of the earth resting on pillars (1 Samuel 2:8).

n: He can command the sun not to rise and seal up the stars so they don’t shine.
God alone stretched out the heavens and walks on the waves of the sea. Christians may think of Jesus walking on the water.

f.w: treadeth upon the waves of the sea

n: He made the great constellations. Ancient people watched these star groups to mark the seasons.

f.g: Probably the Great Bear (Big Dipper); the exact identification is uncertain.

n: He does great things beyond understanding, wonders without number. Job repeats Eliphaz’s words (Job 5:9), but with a darker tone.
God passes right by, yet Job can’t see Him. He feels God is near but hidden — a common experience in suffering.

f.w: he goeth by me, and I see him not

n: If God takes something away, who can stop Him or question Him?
God doesn’t hold back His anger; even the helpers of Rahab bow beneath Him. Rahab here is a mythic sea monster, a symbol of chaos — not the woman of Jericho.

f.g: Hebrew “helpers of Rahab,” a mythic chaos monster God defeated (Isaiah 51:9).

n: How then could I possibly answer Him or find the right words to argue my case?
Even if I were innocent, I couldn’t answer; I could only beg my judge for mercy.
Even if He answered me, I wouldn’t believe He was really listening. Job’s trust is badly shaken.
He crushes me with a storm and multiplies my wounds for no reason. Job doesn’t know it, but the narrator agrees — the suffering truly was “without cause” (Job 2:3).
He won’t even let me catch my breath, but fills me with bitterness.
If it’s a matter of strength, He is strong. If it’s a matter of justice, who can summon Him to court?

f.w: set me a time to plead
f.g: Summon Him to a court hearing.

n: If I declare myself right, my own words would seem to condemn me. In an unequal contest, even innocence can’t be proven.
I am blameless, Job says — but I no longer care about myself; I loathe my life.

f.w: yet would I not know my soul
f.g: I don’t care about myself anymore.

n: It’s all the same, Job says: God destroys both the blameless and the wicked. He is wrestling with the fact that suffering seems to strike good and bad alike.

f.w: He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked

n: When disaster brings sudden death, God seems to mock the despair of the innocent. These are the words of a man in anguish, not a settled doctrine.
The world seems handed over to the wicked, and judges are blindfolded. If God isn’t responsible, then who is?

f.w: covereth the faces of the judges
f.g: Blinds judges so they can’t see justice.

n: Job’s days race by faster than a royal courier and see nothing good.
They pass like fast papyrus boats or an eagle swooping on its prey.

f.g: Light boats made of papyrus reeds.

n: If Job tries to forget his complaint and put on a cheerful face...
...he still dreads his suffering, sure that God will not declare him innocent.
If I’m already judged guilty, why bother trying?
Even if he washed with snow and cleansed his hands with soap...

f.w: make my hands never so clean
f.g: Literally “cleanse my hands with lye” — strong soap.

n: ...God would plunge him into a filthy pit, so that even his own clothes would be disgusted by him. Job feels no effort could make him clean before God.
God is not a man like me, Job says, that we could meet as equals in court.

f.w: he is not a man, as I am

n: Job longs for a “daysman” — an umpire who could put one hand on God and one on Job and bring them together. Christians see this longing answered in Jesus Christ, the Mediator who is both God and man.

f.g: An umpire or mediator — one who sets a day for a hearing and judges between two parties.

f.w: lay his hand upon us both

n: If only God would take away His rod and stop terrifying him!
Then Job could speak without fear. But as things are, he cannot. The chapter ends with Job still longing to meet God face to face.

f.w: but it is not so with me
